title: James Baldwin vs. William F. Buckley Jr. at the Cambridge Union (February 18, 1965)
context: Authentic reconstruction of the historic Cambridge Union Society debate held on February 18, 1965, at Cambridge University on the motion 'The American Dream is at the expense of the American Negro.' Features Cambridge Union President Peter Fullerton presiding, student proposer Mr. David Heycock (Pembroke College), student opposer Mr. Jeremy Burford (Emmanuel College), guest proposer James Baldwin, and guest opposer William F. Buckley Jr. Traces the opening proposition on racial history and economic labor, Buckley's conservative counter-argument invoking Western civilization and individual responsibility, intense philosophical confrontation over cultural reality versus institutional morality, and the overwhelming 544-164 floor division.

metadata.location: Cambridge Union Debating Chamber, Cambridge, England
metadata.motion: The American Dream is at the expense of the American Negro

turns.speaker: Cambridge Union President
turns.text: The House will come to order. The motion before the Cambridge Union tonight is: 'That the American Dream is at the expense of the American Negro.' Speaking first to propose the motion is Mr. David Heycock of Pembroke College, followed by Mr. Jeremy Burford of Emmanuel College to oppose; our distinguished guest speakers are Mr. James Baldwin for the Proposition and Mr. William F. Buckley Jr. for the Opposition.

turns.speaker: Mr. Heycock
turns.text: Mr. President, honorable guests, and members of the House. In proposing this motion, we do not deny the material abundance of the United States, nor the rhetoric of liberty enshrined in its founding charters. Rather, we ask at whose cost that prosperous dream was constructed. From the plantations of Virginia and the cotton fields of the South to the segregated ghettos of Harlem and Chicago, the wealth and leisure that sustain the American Dream were extracted directly from the unpaid labor, disenfranchisement, and systemic exclusion of the American Negro.

turns.speaker: James Baldwin
turns.text: Good evening. I find myself, not for the first time, in the position of a kind of Jeremiah. It would seem to me the proposition before the House is whether the American Dream is at the expense of the American Negro—and one's response to that question has to depend on where you find yourself in the world, what your sense of reality is, what your system of reality is. From the point of view of the man in the Harlem barbershop, Bobby Kennedy only got here yesterday, and now he is already on his way to the presidency—while we have been here four hundred years! I picked the cotton, and I carried it to market, and I built the railroads under someone else's whip, for nothing. For nothing.

turns.speaker: Mr. Burford
turns.text: Mr. President, I rise to oppose the motion. No serious person denies the historical tragedy of slavery or the continuing injustices of Southern segregation. Yet the proposition confuses a tragic historical failure with the essence of the American Dream itself. The American Dream—liberty under law, individual advancement, constitutional rights, and economic opportunity—was not forged at the expense of the Negro; rather, every step toward civil rights legislation, judicial desegregation, and material uplift for black Americans draws directly upon the moral logic and legal machinery of that very American Dream.

turns.speaker: William F. Buckley Jr.
turns.text: Mr. President, Mr. Baldwin, gentlemen of the Cambridge Union. It is impossible to deal with the moral indictment posed by Mr. Baldwin without distinguishing between the sins of individual citizens or regional prejudice and the achievements of American civilization. The American Dream did not depend upon the subjugation of the Negro; indeed, the vast industrial wealth of the United States grew most rapidly in the free North and West through innovation, individual enterprise, and European institutional inheritance. If white Americans carry a moral obligation to dismantle legal barriers to voting and equal opportunity, that obligation arises from the Judeo-Christian and Western principles that constitute the Dream itself.

turns.speaker: William F. Buckley Jr.
turns.text: We must also examine the responsibility of individuals and communities in facing modern realities. Simply indicting the entire white Western world as hopelessly blind or morally bankrupt does not tell a young Negro in Harlem or Mississippi how to acquire the education, civic habits, and economic self-reliance necessary to take his rightful place in a free society. Civilization is hard won, and tearing down its cultural foundations in the name of collective guilt will destroy the very framework within which equality can be won.

turns.speaker: James Baldwin
turns.text: It is a terrible thing for an entire people to surrender to the notion that one-ninth of its population is beneath them—and that assumption is a prison for the American white man just as it is a torment for the Negro! When a sheriff in Mississippi cattle-prods a citizen trying to register to vote, or when a white child learns in his bones that he is not my brother, that is not an accidental departure from Western civilization—it is the price white Americans have paid to avoid facing who they are. You cannot ask the victim who built the country and is still denied his humanity to wait patiently for your civilization to grow a conscience while his children are burned out of churches and trapped in segregated schools.

turns.speaker: William F. Buckley Jr.
turns.text: I yield to no one in condemning the brutality of Bull Connor or the murder of civil rights workers in Mississippi, and I support federal enforcement of the Fifteenth Amendment so every qualified citizen may vote. But when Mr. Baldwin turns from concrete legal injustice to declare that white civilization is irredeemably implicated in white supremacy, he overlooks the self-correcting capacity of Western law and asks the House to embrace a fatalistic despair. What precisely does Mr. Baldwin propose if white Americans are incapable of seeing him as a brother—except the repudiation of the very civilization that gave us Shakespeare, Locke, and the Supreme Court?

turns.speaker: Mr. Heycock
turns.text: With respect to Mr. Buckley, the Opposition misses Mr. Baldwin's central truth: it is precisely the myth of American innocence—the comforting illusion that segregation is merely an isolated regional defect rather than a structural pillar of national life—that perpetuates the expense paid by the American Negro. Until white America confronts the psychological and economic cost of its prosperity, legal reforms alone remain incomplete.

turns.speaker: Mr. Burford
turns.text: And yet if the House votes that the American Dream itself exists solely at the Negro's expense, it endorses a historical indictment that discounts the massive progress achieved through constitutional reform, the 1964 Civil Rights Act, and the shared aspirations of millions of black and white citizens striving for individual dignity inside the American framework.

turns.speaker: James Baldwin
turns.text: I am not asking to be given something; I am saying that what you call your civilization has never yet taken the risk of treating me as a human being. I am not an exotic spectator in America—I helped build it, my blood is in its soil, and until the moment comes when white Americans recognize that the American Negro is not a problem to be managed by your conscience, but a man whose fate defines your own soul, the American Dream remains a nightmare for those who paid for it.

turns.speaker: William F. Buckley Jr.
turns.text: Let the House remember that the only way the Negro can triumph in America is not by overturning the institutions of Western liberty or declaring perpetual racial estrangement, but by demanding full citizenship and individual responsibility within the constitutional order. If white America must abandon prejudice, black leadership too must resist turning understandable grievance into an ideology that despairs of reconciliation.

turns.speaker: Cambridge Union President
turns.text: The debate has reached its conclusion, and the House will now divide on the motion: 'That the American Dream is at the expense of the American Negro.' Brief final words from our seconders and guests before the Tellers record the division.

turns.speaker: Mr. Heycock
turns.text: The Proposition rests on the undeniable historical truth articulated by James Baldwin: American prosperity and national innocence were purchased at the price of black subjugation, and conscience demands that the House affirm this motion.

turns.speaker: Mr. Burford
turns.text: The Opposition asks the House to reject an indictment of the entire American Dream and affirm instead that liberty under law remains the Negro's surest instrument of emancipation.

turns.speaker: James Baldwin
turns.text: If my countrymen cannot face the truth of our history and see that my survival is bound up with theirs, then the Dream collapses of its own moral blindness. I beg the House to vote Aye.

turns.speaker: William F. Buckley Jr.
turns.text: Civilization advances through individual responsibility, constitutional justice, and reason, not collective indictment. I urge the House to vote No.

turns.speaker: Cambridge Union President
turns.text: Order! The Tellers have returned the result of the division on the motion 'That the American Dream is at the expense of the American Negro': Ayes, 544; Noes, 164. The motion is overwhelmingly carried by 380 votes. The House stands adjourned.
